Callous

/KAL-us/ — stress on first syllable, rhymes with pal us · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Someone who is callous shows no concern for other people's pain and acts without sympathy toward them.

Laughing at the injured player was a callous thing to do.

Worked Example

When the homeless man asked for directions, pedestrians hurried past without answering, showing a callous indifference to his distress.

Callous captures the hardened, unfeeling quality of not caring about someone's suffering. This is more precise than 'rude' (which could be unintentional), 'mean' (which could be impulsive), or 'cold' (which could simply mean emotionally distant). Callous specifically names a chronic, hardened lack of sympathy.

How Callous Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

cruel

cruel: deliberately causing pain to other people

heartless

heartless: completely lacking pity or warmth

indifferent

indifferent: simply not caring one way or another

Antonyms

compassionate

compassionate: feeling deep concern for others' suffering

empathetic

empathetic: sharing and understanding another person's feelings

How Strong Is It? — distant → indifferent → heartless → callous

distant vs. callous

distant vs. callous: Distant is far weaker than callous: a distant person merely keeps to themselves, while a callous person is hardened against other people's pain.

indifferent vs. callous

indifferent vs. callous: Indifferent is weaker than callous; an indifferent person simply doesn't care much, but a callous person stays unmoved even when faced with real suffering.

heartless vs. callous

heartless vs. callous: Heartless is nearly as strong as callous, but callous caps this scale: heartless means lacking pity, while callous suggests someone so hardened over time that others' pain no longer registers at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — call (callus)

Root — call (callus): hard skin (Latin)

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: full of, having the quality of (Latin (-osus))

Put it together

Put it together: Callous literally means 'full of hard skin.' Just as a callus is skin toughened until it can barely feel, a callous person has grown emotionally thick-skinned — hardened until other people's pain no longer touches them.

Use the root in a new word: callus

Use the root in a new word: callus: Years of guitar practice left a callus on each of her fingertips — the same Latin word for 'hard skin' that makes a callous person emotionally hardened and unfeeling.

Word Building

Word Choice

neutral / everyday

Callous is best for describing someone's hardened lack of concern or sympathy for others' suffering — an emotional toughness or indifference that seems cruel. Use it when someone shows no compassion despite obvious pain or need. For unintentional rudeness or simple emotional distance, 'cold' or 'distant' is more appropriate.
